newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany plans to cut pensions, raise inputs.
newsitem.headline: Germany plans to cut pensions, raise inputs.

text.p: Germany must cut pensions, raise contributions and set up a tax-financed "Family Fund" to keep its state pensions scheme going into the 21st century, a coalition policy group proposed on Monday.

A pensions commission chaired by Labour Minister Norbert Bluem recommended cutting pensions to 64 percent of average net wages by the year 2030. Contributions would rise to 22.9 percent of wages over the same period.

To keep Germany's compulsory state pensions scheme afloat and prevent the value of old-age pay from being eroded, some welfare payments -- like maternity benefits -- now funded by pension contributions would be transferred to the Family Fund.
Reaffirming his commitment to Germany's pensions model, Bluem said: "The pensions insurance scheme is adaptable and can cope with future needs."

Pensions are now around 70 percent of net wages, a level too high to cope with the "greying" of Germany's 80 million population. The report said the number of Germans aged over 65 would rise to 20 million by 2030, up from 12.5 million in 1996.
The shifting demographic balance has already forced up pension charges -- one of many labour overheads seen deterring job creation in Germany's unemployment-hit economy.
Pension charges were just 17.5 percent as recently as 1993 but Bonn put them up to a record 20.3 percent this year after reserves fell below the statutory minimum one month cover.

Without reform, the commission said that maintaining current real pension levels would consume over a quarter of net wages by 2030. With the suggested restructuring, contributions would fall to 18.7 percent by 2010 before rising again.

Bluem's bid to rejig pensions has run headlong into Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans, announced last week, to slash 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in income and corporate taxes by 1999 to boost investment and jobs.

The pensions commission opposed Waigel's plans to tax pensions. Bluem -- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's longest-serving minister -- also wants a two-point hike in value-added tax to help finance the Family Fund.
There was one dissenting voice on the commission, that of Meinhard Miegel, head of the influential Institute for Economy and Society, who said its assumptions on unemployment were too optimistic.
The existing system "cannot convincingly solve" problems thrown up by changing demographics and worsening employment prospects, Miegel said in a lone minority report.
Bluem's report now goes for review by the three parties of Kohl's 14-year centre-right government, and heavy revisions are likely before legislation is drafted.
After last week's tax row, the embattled minister won much-needed support from senior colleagues on Monday.

"Norbert Bluem has a very tough task to master with the reform of the social security and in particularly the pensions system. But he has our full support," said Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
Schaeuble did, however, call Bluem's linking of the tax and pensions issues "unfortunate". He did not rule out raising other indirect levies like petrol tax instead of VAT, however.
Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), hitherto adamant opponents of raising indirect taxes, said they would not oppose discussing a moderate VAT increase.
